items.title: Neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease: From glial cell states and molecular networks to biomarkers and precision therapeutics.
items.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is now recognized as a biologically heterogeneous syndrome in which amyloid-β pathology, Tau-related alterations, and neuroinflammation are key interconnected processes. Microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, complement, inflammasomes, neurovascular cells, and peripheral immunity are implicated as both adaptive and disease-promoting contributors to the pathophysiology of AD. Here, we highlight mechanisms by which innate immunity and peripheral immune cells influence amyloid β-peptide metabolism, Tau pathophysiology, excitatory synaptic function, oxidative stress response, blood-brain barrier integrity, and systemic inflammation in the context of Alzheimer's disease. A particular focus is made on the role of TREM2-related microglial function and the NLRP3 inflammasome, complement-mediated synaptic pruning, astrocyte crosstalk, and the limitations of the M1/M2 and A1/A2 concepts. A distinction is made between biomarkers of core AD pathophysiology and those specific to neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. An emphasis is placed on the clinical utility of plasma p-tau217 in combination with Aβ42/Aβ40, GFAP, NfL, sTREM2, YKL-40, and neuroinflammation imaging. With respect to therapeutics, an effort is made to focus on the need to harness desirable inflammatory pathways while specifically targeting deleterious processes rather than adopting an overarching anti-inflammatory approach. Single-cell, spatial, multi-omics, and biomarker-driven approaches may enable patient stratification based on underlying pathophysiology, allowing for stage-specific combination therapeutic strategies. Overall, studies presented in this review highlight a precision-neuroimmunology concept in which neuroinflammatory processes are both triggers and effectors of disease pathology and can be selectively modulated for clinical benefit.

items.title: Melatonin ameliorates behavioral deficits in 5xFAD mice through modulation of neurogenesis, neuroimmune responses, neurotransmission, and metabolic pathways.
items.authors: Jaydeep Roy; Ka Chun Tsui; Chi Him Poon; Jingyi Zhang; Yunfan Lai; Kan Yin Wong; Mazel Mihardja; Vera Tse
items.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder with limited disease-modifying treatment options. Melatonin, an endogenous hormone, has been shown to have therapeutic effects on amyloid deposition, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation in AD. However, the mechanisms of its neuroprotective effects in the hippocampus remain largely unknown. This study aimed to investigate the multi-mechanistic neuroprotective effects of melatonin in AD. Eight-month-old female 5xFAD transgenic mice were treated with melatonin (10 mg/kg) for 4 weeks. Temozolomide and bromodeoxyuridine were used to block neurogenesis and to label proliferating neurons, respectively. Our results showed that 5xFAD mice treated with melatonin exhibited improved exploratory behavior, enhanced memory performance, reduced depressive-like symptoms, and decreased levels of stress hormones. At the molecular level, melatonin reduced amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaque accumulation, elevated hippocampal neurogenesis markers (DCX and BrdU), increased Trem2 expression and anti-inflammatory microglial activation, restored serotonergic, dopaminergic, catecholaminergic, and GABAergic neurotransmission, and partially normalized broader hippocampal metabolic pathways. Notably, temozolomide treatment abrogated the beneficial effects of melatonin on memory performance and depressive-like behavior in 5xFAD mice, indicating a neurogenesis-dependent mechanism. Collectively, these findings suggest that melatonin ameliorates behavioral deficits in 5xFAD mice through both neurogenesis-independent (reduced Aβ plaque accumulation, Trem2-microglial activation, neurotransmission restoration, and metabolic remodeling) and hippocampal neurogenesis-dependent mechanisms. Overall, melatonin holds therapeutic potential for attenuating the neuropathology and behavioral deficits in AD.

items.title: Molecular Signatures of HIV-Induced Neuroinflammation and Neurodegeneration in Human Cerebral Organoids: Identification of Therapeutic Targets for NeuroHIV.
items.authors: Karthick Chennakesavan; Malaroviyam Samikkannu; Shreyan Gupta; Olasunkanmi Israel Tayo; Arpan Acharya; James J Cai; Siddappa N Byrareddy; Thangavel Samikkannu
items.abstract: HIV-associated neurological complications remain a major concern in people living with HIV (PWH), even under effective viral suppression with combination antiretroviral therapy (cART), underscoring unresolved mechanisms driving HIV-related neurodegeneration. To address this gap, we used HIV-1-infected human cerebral organoids (hCOs) containing microglia as a physiologically relevant three-dimensional model of the central nervous system (CNS) and validated key findings in the brain region of simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV)-infected, cART-treated rhesus macaque model. Integrated single-nucleus RNA sequencing with ATAC-seq (multi-omics), identifies cell-type-specific alterations in dual innate immune-driven inflammatory signaling pathways across neural and glial populations in hCOs. Microglia were preferentially infected and activated, initiating IL-17A-mediated cascades involving IFN-γ/STAT1, CEBPB, and NF-κB signaling. These pathways converged with cGAS-STING and Notch-NEURL1 signaling, both associated with neuroinflammation and synaptic dysfunction. cART suppressed viral replication, reduced IL-17A-mediated neuroinflammation, improved mitochondrial function, and restored synaptic gene expression. Collectively, these findings identify dysregulation of IL-17A, STAT1, CEBPB, and cGAS-STING signaling as key molecular drivers of HIV-associated neuroinflammation. They also establish a potential mechanistic link between IL-17A signaling and microglial remodeling, providing a translational framework for the development of CNS-targeted therapies in PWH.

items.title: An aging-sensitive secreted phospholipase confers neuroprotection and cognitive resilience.
items.authors: Cinzia Vicidomini; Travis D Goode; Ruilin Yu; Iyanah Mehta; Kathleen M McAvoy; Connor H Beveridge; Caitlin E Randolph; Sanjay N Iyer
items.abstract: Cognitive reserve theory posits that compensatory mechanisms during aging stave off cognitive decline and lower risk for Alzheimer's disease. Here, in a screen for hippocampal dentate granule cell (DGC) synapse loss-induced factors in mice, we identified a secreted phospholipase, Pla2g2f, whose expression increases in DGCs during aging and is associated with cognitive resilience in humans. Pla2g2f deletion in DGCs exacerbates aging-associated pathophysiological changes, including synapse loss, inflammatory microglia, reactive astrogliosis, impaired neurogenesis, lipid dysregulation, lipid droplet accumulation and hippocampal-dependent memory loss. Conversely, boosting Pla2g2f in DGCs during aging is sufficient to prevent these pathophysiological alterations in hippocampal-cortical circuits, protect memory and prophylactically modify trajectory of cognitive decline. Mutagenesis of the catalytic site of PLA2G2F prevented lipid droplet mobilization and reduction of reactive gliosis and inflammatory microglia. Neuronal PLA2G2F mediates intercellular signaling to decrease lipid droplet and cholesterol ester load in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia. Our findings implicate PLA2G2F as a compensatory neuroprotective broadcast signal that maintains lipid homeostasis to counteract aging-associated cognitive decline.

items.title: Akkermansia muciniphila gavage alleviates depression-like behaviors in female A53T α-synuclein transgenic mice.
items.authors: Shuyu Li; Xingkun Chu; Rui Deng; Wei Zheng; Xinyuan Suo; Guangqiang Sun; Hongchun Liu; Meiyu Geng
items.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized not only by progressive motor deficits but also by non-motor symptoms, such as depression, which often emerge during the prodromal stage and significantly impair quality of life. While Akkermansia muciniphila (AKK) has shown potential in modulating neuroinflammation, its specific role and underlying mechanisms in alleviating PD-associated non-motor symptoms remain unclear. In this study, we investigated the effects of AKK intervention in 16-month-old female A53T α-synuclein (α-syn) transgenic mice. Behavioral assessments revealed that oral administration of AKK significantly ameliorated depression-like behaviors, evidenced by reduced immobility in the forced swim test and increased sucrose preference, without affecting motor function, spatial memory, or gastrointestinal motility. items.title: Creatine preserves mitochondrial integrity and ameliorates early epileptiform activity and cognitive impairment via regulation of Na⁺,K⁺-ATPase in adolescent rats with severe traumatic brain injury.
items.authors: Luiz Fernando Freire Royes; Guilherme Lago Busanello; Douglas Buchmann Godinho; Gustavo Cassol; Alexandre Seixas Nascimento; Gabriel Correa Lima; Jane do Socorro Dos Navegantes Marçal Cunha; Marcia Consentino Kronka Sosthenes
items.abstract: In this study, we demonstrate for the first time that post-injury creatine supplementation (300 mg/kg, p.o.) administered for two weeks attenuates blood-brain barrier disruption, cortical lesion volume (by ∼60%), spatial memory deficits (reducing escape latency by ∼50% in the Barnes maze), hippocampal theta/delta rhythm alterations, and epileptiform activity in 35-day-old male rats subjected to severe fluid percussion injury (FPI). In the hippocampus, the FPI protocol did not cause overt neuronal loss-particularly of parvalbumin-positive neurons in the CA1 and CA2 regions-but it significantly reduced creatine levels and induced marked mitochondrial dysfunction. These alterations were evidenced by impaired MTT reduction, disrupted mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψ), decreased SDH activity, inhibition of respiratory chain complexes I-III, COX, citrate synthase (CS), and CKm activity, together with increased mitochondrial oxidative stress (enhanced DCFH-DA oxidation, elevated 4-hydroxynonenal levels, depletion of free -SH groups, and reduced GSH levels). We propose a mechanistic cascade wherein mitochondrial dysfunction and elevated oxidative stress drive the inhibition of Na⁺,K⁺-ATPase, which in turn contributes to neuronal hyperexcitability and cognitive deficits. Creatine's ability to maintain mitochondrial integrity directly interrupts this cascade, protecting against dysfunctions in these essential ion-gradient systems. In conclusion, post-injury creatine supplementation preserves mitochondrial function, maintains Na⁺,K⁺-ATPase activity, and prevents epileptiform activity and cognitive deficits, highlighting creatine as a promising strategy to mitigate secondary injury. However, these findings must be interpreted in light of certain limitations, including the use of a male-only cohort, a single time-point assessment, and the correlational nature of the proposed mechanistic pathways, warranting further investigation.

items.title: Outcomes of Allogeneic Stem Cell Transplantation in a North American Adult T Cell Leukemia/Lymphoma Cohort.
items.authors: Trent Peng Wang; Julie Nguyen; Leticia Campoverde; Jeremy Ramdial; Luis Malpica; Matthew Hamby; Stefan Klaus Barta; Nyein Nyein Thaw Dar
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is an and aggressive mature T-cell neoplasm driven by human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1) with dismal prognosis. North American ATLL (NA-ATLL) disproportionately impacts individuals of Afro-Caribbean and Latin American descent who face significant disparities in identifying conventional 8/8 HLA-matched donors in international registries. While allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) is established in East Asian cohorts, outcomes data in Western populations remain limited. We aimed to evaluate post-HCT survival, toxicities, and prognostic risk factors in NA-ATLL. OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to evaluate HCT clinical outcomes. Our primary outcome was overall survival (OS), and secondary outcomes included progression-free survival (PFS), non-relapse mortality (NRM), and graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). We tested the hypotheses that alternative donor HCT yields comparable survival to matched donor HCT and assessed variables that may dictate post-transplant survival. STUDY DESIGN: This was a multicenter retrospective registry study evaluating 46 adult patients with NA-ATLL who underwent allogeneic HCT across participating North American centers. Myeloablative conditioning regimens were myeloablative in 21.7%, and alternative donor HCT (without a matched donor) were used in 54.3%. Survival endpoints (OS, PFS) were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared via log-rank tests. Cumulative incidences of relapse, NRM, acute GVHD, and chronic GVHD were calculated considering competing risks. Independent prognostic variables were evaluated using Cox multivariable proportional hazards regression analysis. RESULTS: There was no significant difference in OS or PFS between those who received matched versus alternative donor HCT (OS p = 0.601, PFS p = 0.376). Patients with acute disease subtype had worse OS compared to lymphomatous (logrank p = 0.043, 3-year OS 22.2% versus 52.3%, respectively). Acute GVHD yielded a 1-year cumulative incidence rate of 45.7% (95%CI; 30.7-59.5%) while that of chronic GVHD was 18.5% (95%CI; 8.5-31.5%). Twenty-seven patients were deceased at time of analysis, primarily due to relapse-related causes in 17 patients. In multivariable analysis, lymphomatous disease subtype (HR 0.3, 95%CI 0.1-0.88, p = 0.027) and Karnofsky performance score of ≥80 (HR 0.26, 95%CI 0.09-0.73, p = 0.01) were significant predictors of OS. CONCLUSION: This is the largest cohort evaluating HCT outcomes in a NA-ATLL population. Alternative donor HCT may expand access to HCT without an apparent increase in non-relapse mortality in this selected cohort. Clinical acute disease subtype shows inferior outcomes compared to lymphomatous subtype. Baseline performance status is a predictor of improved prognosis post-transplant. These data suggest that fit patients should proceed to HCT expeditiously with any donor option available.

items.title: Immune biomarkers of response and resistance to ipilimumab and nivolumab in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer.
items.authors: Apostolia M Tsimberidou; Christopher R Cabanski; Alexandra Drakaki; Danny N Khalil; Bilal A Siddiqui; Sreyashi Basu; Kwame Okrah; Diane M Da Silva
items.abstract: Immune checkpoint therapies have shown limited efficacy in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). The AMADEUS prostate expansion cohort (NCT03651271) evaluated the efficacy, safety, and biomarkers of escalating ipilimumab doses combined with nivolumab. Patients received ipilimumab 1 milligram per kilogram (mg/kg) + nivolumab 360 mg (I1+N360), ipilimumab 3 mg/kg + nivolumab 1 mg/kg (I3+N1), or ipilimumab 5 mg/kg + nivolumab 1 mg/kg (I5+N1). Coprimary endpoints were 6-month disease control rate (DCR) and changes in tumoral CD8 percentage. Thirty-two patients were enrolled. DCRs were 33% (4 of 12) for I1+N360, 20% (1 of 5) for I3+N1, and 20% (3 of 15) for I5+N1. Across cohorts, tumoral CD8 percentage increased by a median of 5.0%. Although higher ipilimumab doses were tolerable, I1+N360 achieved similar disease control and immune activation with a more favorable safety profile. Early disease progression was associated with increased expression of a TREM2-associated myeloid gene signature, which was also significantly enriched in two independent prostate cancer datasets.

items.title: Microtubules and nuclear pores position centromeres and genes in neural stem cells.
items.abstract: Chromatin's spatial organization is important for cell division, epigenetic memory, and gene regulation. Chromatin architecture is often reflected in nonrandom centromere positioning, which changes during development and disease. However, the mechanisms and functions of centromere positioning remain largely unknown. Here, we report that Drosophila neural stem cells cluster centromeres near the nuclear envelope, adjacent to the apical centrosome. This asymmetric centromere positioning persists throughout interphase but is lost in differentiated progeny. Asymmetric centromere positioning is regulated by microtubules from the apical centrosome connected to nuclear pore complexes (NPCs), generating a pulling force mediated by the motor protein Dynein and its binding partner Mushroom body defect. Lamin facilitates centromere-NPC binding, necessary for centromere positioning and clustering. We also find that the developmentally regulated genes hunchback and pendulin occupy specific nuclear regions, correlating with polarized centromere localization. We propose that fly neural stem cells translate their inherent polarity into stereotypical chromatin organization, potentially influencing cell-fate decisions and stem cell behavior.

items.title: P-body-mediated RNA decay controls neural crest EMT.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
items.authors: Arvind Arul Nambi Rajan; Michael L Piacentino; Marianne E Bronner; Erica J Hutchins
items.abstract: Neural crest cells, a multipotent vertebrate stem cell population, undergo a tightly regulated epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) to delaminate from the neural tube and initiate migration. Neural crest EMT is controlled by a transient pulse of Draxin, which acts as a molecular rheostat of canonical Wnt signaling, and is then rapidly downregulated by unknown mechanisms. To address this, here we use in vivo reporter assays and live RNA imaging to show that Draxin mRNA is rapidly degraded posttranscriptionally via its 3' untranslated region. We found that Draxin transcripts are targeted to cytoplasmic processing bodies (P-bodies), which are membrane-less sites of RNA processing and decay. Disruption of P-bodies by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated depletion of the RNA helicase DDX6 prevented posttranscriptional downregulation of Draxin and impaired neural crest EMT in vivo. These findings parallel observations in human patients carrying DDX6 mutations, who exhibit defects in P-body assembly and craniofacial abnormalities associated with neural crest dysfunction. Together, our results identify P-bodies as regulators of Draxin mRNA decay and reveal a spatially organized mechanism of RNA turnover that controls neural crest EMT during vertebrate development.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Preclinical and first-in-human evaluation of VG-3927/SAR448851, an oral small-molecule TREM2 agonist for Alzheimer's disease.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Borislav Dejanovic; Matthew D Figley; Elizabeth Weisman; Beril Kiragasi; Frederick W Gergits; Kelley Larson; Abigail Renoux; Raj Rajagovindan
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Microglial dysfunction is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis, with loss-of-function variants in the microglial receptor TREM2 as major risk factors for late-onset AD. We report VG-3927, an oral, CNS-penetrant small-molecule TREM2 agonist that engages the transmembrane domains of TREM2 and its adaptor DAP12 to promote higher-order receptor complex formation and downstream signaling. VG-3927 and tool compound VG-3909 exhibited (sub)nanomolar potency, cooperated with endogenous ligands including amyloid-β (Aβ), and restored signaling in disease-associated TREM2 variants. In human iPSC-derived neuron-microglia-astrocyte cultures, VG-3927 reduced inflammatory cytokines and markers of neuronal damage. In 5xFAD amyloidosis mice expressing the common variant of hTREM2 (5xFAD;hTREM2CV), VG-3909 induced neuroprotective transcriptional reprogramming of microglia, particularly in the plaque niche; enhanced Aβ phagocytosis; and boosted brain glucose metabolism. By contrast, a TREM2 agonist antibody, which may be sequestered by soluble TREM2 (sTREM2), failed to engage plaque microglia. In a first-in-human, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 1 trial (NCT06343636, n = 115), VG-3927 was well tolerated across single and multiple ascending doses of up to 140 milligrams. Pharmacokinetics supported once-daily dosing with high CNS penetration (CSF-to-unbound plasma ratio of 0.91). VG-3927 induced dose-dependent reductions in CSF sTREM2, a biomarker of target engagement, consistent across healthy and elderly participants and participants with AD, supporting further clinical development in AD under the new designation SAR448851.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: An aging-sensitive secreted phospholipase confers neuroprotection and cognitive resilience.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Cinzia Vicidomini; Travis D Goode; Ruilin Yu; Iyanah Mehta; Kathleen M McAvoy; Connor H Beveridge; Caitlin E Randolph; Sanjay N Iyer
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Cognitive reserve theory posits that compensatory mechanisms during aging stave off cognitive decline and lower risk for Alzheimer's disease. Here, in a screen for hippocampal dentate granule cell (DGC) synapse loss-induced factors in mice, we identified a secreted phospholipase, Pla2g2f, whose expression increases in DGCs during aging and is associated with cognitive resilience in humans. Pla2g2f deletion in DGCs exacerbates aging-associated pathophysiological changes, including synapse loss, inflammatory microglia, reactive astrogliosis, impaired neurogenesis, lipid dysregulation, lipid droplet accumulation and hippocampal-dependent memory loss. Conversely, boosting Pla2g2f in DGCs during aging is sufficient to prevent these pathophysiological alterations in hippocampal-cortical circuits, protect memory and prophylactically modify trajectory of cognitive decline. Mutagenesis of the catalytic site of PLA2G2F prevented lipid droplet mobilization and reduction of reactive gliosis and inflammatory microglia. Neuronal PLA2G2F mediates intercellular signaling to decrease lipid droplet and cholesterol ester load in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia. Our findings implicate PLA2G2F as a compensatory neuroprotective broadcast signal that maintains lipid homeostasis to counteract aging-associated cognitive decline.

top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Vidyalakshmi Chandramohan; James E Herndon; Anjali Barnwal; Katayoun Ayasoufi; Weixuan Yan; Kevin Stevenson; Michelle L Bowie; Michael C Brown
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: D2C7-ATC is a recombinant antibody-toxin conjugate (ATC) targeting wild-type epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and mutant EGFR variant III (EGFRvIII). We conducted a single-arm, single-site, open-label phase 1 trial evaluating a single infusion of D2C7-ATC via convection-enhanced delivery in the enhancing disease of 81 patients with biopsy-confirmed recurrent malignant glioma. The primary objective was to determine toxicity and the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) of D2C7-ATC. Secondary objectives included describing overall survival (OS) and assessing the association between EGFR expression and OS. top_journal_neuroscience.title: Elp1 is required for myeloid differentiation and brain repopulation.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Marius Marc-Daniel Mader; Wanhua Li; Alexa Scavetti; Yongjin Yoo; Gernot Neumayer; Katie Han; Yohei Shibuya; Michael Haney
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Haematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) transplantation-mediated replacement of microglia-the reconstitution of the central nervous system microglial niche with donor-derived myeloid cells-represents a promising strategy for brain cell therapies1-7. However, the cell-intrinsic molecular regulators of HSPC-derived myeloid lineage commitment in the brain have remained largely uncharacterized. This is partially because the scarcity of primary HSPCs has rendered large-scale genetic interrogation intractable. Here we explored whether ex vivo expansion of primary cultured HSPCs (cHSPCs) enables unbiased genetic interrogation of haematopoietic differentiation. We established that cHSPCs can be genetically manipulated and readily differentiate into myeloid cells and repopulate microglia niches of the brain after transplantation. Moreover, primary neonatal astrocytes contained strong signals to induce myeloid specification of cHSPCs in vitro. To identify genes that regulate glia-induced myeloid differentiation, we successfully screened around 20,000 individual genetic perturbations and characterized genes involved in the regulation of cell signalling, cell cycle, mitochondrial function and protein translation. Among these genes was elongator acetyltransferase complex subunit 1 (Elp1), which suppressed the unfolded protein response during myeloid specification and was essential for the generation but not maintenance of myeloid cells. Our work establishes a platform to investigate the molecular mechanisms of brain myeloid biology.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Extracellular vesicle α-synuclein topology reveals disease-associated conformers in brain and blood.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Suman Dutta; Amin Atashgaran; Anis Sahoo; Stelios Chatzimichail; Achillefs N Kapanidis; George K Tofaris
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are unified by pathological α-synuclein (αSyn) aggregation, yet diverge in terms of the cellular distribution of pathology and clinical phenotype. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as potential mediators or biomarkers of αSyn pathology, but whether their molecular constituents in the brain reflect disease-specific processes or conformations remains unknown. Here, we combined EV isolation, electrochemiluminescence, quantitative mass spectrometry and nanoscale single-vesicle imaging by direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) to map the topology, epitope exposure and cellular origin of αSyn in EVs isolated from post-mortem PD, DLB, MSA, and healthy control (HC) brains and assessed the tractability of these molecular signatures in blood. Proteomics and immunoblotting of EV lysates isolated from human brains confirmed that they were highly purified and derived from neurons and glial cell subtypes. Across diseases, αSyn association with EVs exhibited distinct patterns: In PD and DLB, both total αSyn levels normalised to CD81 and the percentage of neuronal (L1CAM+) EVs with aggregated αSyn as detected by aggregate-preferring antibodies, were increased, whereas in MSA, aggregated αSyn was detected primarily in neuronal and to a lesser extent glial EV subpopulations without an increase in total EV-associated αSyn. Further epitope mapping by dSTORM identified a distinct αSyn conformational arrangement, as detected by antibodies against an epitope spanning αSyn residues 34-45, that was enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs in MSA compared to PD. This N-terminal immunoreactive conformer was tractable in serum and enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs from MSA compared to PD patients or controls. Collectively, our findings suggest that the epitope accessibility and topology of EV-associated αSyn proteoforms, rather than their abundance alone, discriminate synucleinopathy subtypes, offering a framework for a blood-based conformational stratification of these disorders.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: CHCHD2 mitigates age-associated proteostatic collapse by maintaining homeostasis of the mitochondria-lysosome axis.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: Teresa R Kee; Brianna M Masters; Khoi D Tran; Hanna Jeon; Ma Long; Grace Xu; Sophia A Khan; Edwin Vázquez-Rosa
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Mutations in coiled-coil-helix-coiled-coil-helix domain containing 2 (CHCHD2), including the Parkinson's disease (PD)-linked CHCHD2T61I mutation, are associated with Lewy body disorders (LBDs) by unknown mechanisms. Here, we demonstrate that CHCHD2T61I exacerbates age-related brain pathologies, including axonal degeneration and cognitive deficits, by disrupting the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Specifically, CHCHD2T61I binds and reduces cathepsin B (CTSB) and cathepsin L (CTSL) levels, inducing lysosomal membrane permeability and impairing α-synuclein fibril clearance. We also demonstrate that human CHCHD2 declines in the brain with age, while expression of wild-type CHCHD2 safeguards against age-related neuroinflammation, dopaminergic neuron loss, insoluble protein aggregation, and structural deterioration of mitochondria and lysosomes. These findings, supported by observed reductions in CTSB and CHCHD2 in human LBD brains, establish CHCHD2 as a key regulator of neuronal resilience to aging and proteostatic collapse via the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Preventing age-associated CHCHD2 decline offers a therapeutic strategy to preserve brain health throughout aging.

top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation in the developing human brain remains a central challenge in neuroscience, particularly in transient cell types and developmental stages where data are limited. We present Seal, an interpretable artificial intelligence (AI) transfer learning framework for genome-based modeling of gene expression and variant effects with spatiotemporal resolution across 26 regions, 30 cell types and 7 developmental stages. Seal predictions provide mechanistic interpretation by linking variants to transcriptional regulators in a spatiotemporal context. Applying Seal to genome-wide association studies, we identify shared and distinct regulatory architectures across six neuropsychiatric conditions that align with clinical trajectories. In the Simons Simplex Collection autism cohort whole-genome data, Seal uncovers a significant burden of de novo regulatory variants in transient fetal excitatory neurons, revealing cell-type-specific and stage-specific effects. By connecting genetic variation to spatiotemporal regulatory programs, Seal offers a general framework for uncovering mechanisms of human brain development and disease.

top_journal_neuroscience.title: Personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines in ovarian cancer: a phase 1 trial.
top_journal_neuroscience.authors: MacLean C Sellars; Jessica A Frank; Bohoon Shim; Allison Vanasse; Ruolin Liu; Cleo Forman; Chloe R Tu; Kyohei K Tabata
top_journal_neuroscience.abstract: Personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines in the adjuvant setting are of increasing interest across malignancies. Here we report the results of a phase 1 clinical trial testing the feasibility and safety of personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines for high-grade epithelial ovarian cancer. 'NeoVax' consisted of pools of synthetic long peptides targeting patient-specific neoantigens admixed with the immunostimulant poly-ICLC, was combined with delayed administration of anti-PD-1 antibody, and was tested in ten patients (one newly diagnosed patient (Cohort A) and nine patients at first recurrence (Cohort B)) with platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer following standard-of-care platinum doublet chemotherapy. Nine of 12 evaluable Cohort B patients were vaccinated (75%, 90% CI 47-93%) and 1 of 9 Cohort A patients (11%, 90% CI 0.6-43%). No unexpected safety signals were encountered and no patients discontinued treatment due to toxicity. Across patients, >70% selected targets remained detectable by noninvasive cell-free DNA analysis despite a median of 6.5 months from the time of diagnostic biopsy to vaccine administration, during which, patients received standard-of-care chemotherapy. Biomarker analysis was suggestive of biologic activity of the vaccine in six of ten patients and this was associated with broader tumor and vaccine-specific immune responses in blood and tumor following vaccination. Resistant tumor clones reflected diverse mechanisms affecting antigen presentation, indicative of immune-selective pressure exerted by vaccination. Overall, the interplay between the repertoire of antigens presented by the tumor and the breadth of induced immunity seemed to dictate clinical efficacy following vaccination. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04024878 .

global_hot_topics.title: Predicting IGD treatment outcomes across interventions using a whole-brain functional connectome biomarker.
global_hot_topics.authors: Meiting Wei; Xin Luo; Jiejie Fu; Shuang Li; Haosen Ni; Jiang Liu; Guang-Heng Dong
global_hot_topics.abstract: BACKGROUND: Although treatment approaches have been explored in internet gaming disorder (IGD), however, little is known about the specific neural activity that is associated with treatment outcomes. This study aims to establish a treatment-sensitive network that reliably predicts treatment outcomes across different interventions for IGD. METHODS: Resting-state fMRI data were collected from 90 individuals with IGD who received one of three different intervention protocols (mindfulness meditation, approach bias modification, or retrieval-aversive conditioning training). Connectome-based predictive modelling (CPM) was used to build a treatment-sensitive network to predict individual symptom reduction, then validated them on the external dataset. RESULTS: The negative (r = 0.401, p <.001) and combined network (r = 0.480, p <.001) can significantly predict a reduction of addiction severity (baseline minus post-test). Specifically, the negative network was primarily centred on the motor, subcortical, and salience networks. The positive network primarily involved cerebellar-related connections. Incorporating these into a combined model significantly improved predictive accuracy, suggesting that cerebellar-related connectivity may contribute to the prediction of intervention-related clinical improvement. Finally, the treatment-sensitive network was validated in a separate data. CONCLUSIONS: This study established a treatment-sensitive network based on the whole-brain connectome. These findings provide valuable empirical evidence for identifying biomarkers for IGD treatment and advance personalised therapeutic strategies. CLINICAL TRIALS REGISTRATION: The trial protocol was pre-registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (www.chictr.org.cn; ChiCTR2300077831(MM), ChiCTR2300075869(ApBm), ChiCTR2500095444(R-AC), ChiCTR2400090834(SAE)).

global_hot_topics.title: HoLEP Versus Mini-HoLEP: A Long-term Follow-up Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial.
global_hot_topics.authors: Tomer Mendelson; Omri Schwarztuch Gildor; Ziv Savin; Tarek Taha; Itamar Confino; Tomer Bashi; Karin Lifshitz; Yotam Veredgorn
global_hot_topics.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) is increasingly performed with miniaturized instruments, aiming to reduce postoperative urinary incontinence (UI). Evidence for mini-HoLEP (MiLEP) using a 22-Fr resectoscope remains largely retrospective or nonrandomized. We aimed to compare MiLEP with a standard 26 Fr HoLEP in a prospective randomized trial. METHODS: Ninety men were randomized to MiLEP (n = 45) or HoLEP (n = 45). All procedures were performed by one surgeon using a standardized technique. The prespecified primary end point was UI, defined as any reported loss of urine, at 1 mo. Key secondary end points included UI at 2 mo and at the end of follow-up. KEY FINDINGS AND LIMITATIONS: Median follow-up was 828 days. UI at 1 mo was lower after MiLEP than HoLEP (22.2% vs 51.1%; odds ratio [OR] 0.27; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.11-0.67; p = 0.004). UI at 2 mo was also lower (8.9% vs 24.4%; OR 0.30; 95% CI = 0.09-0.99; p = 0.048), whereas long-term UI did not differ significantly (2.2% vs 6.7%; p = 0.61). MiLEP also lowered the need for meatal dilation (15% vs 51%; p < 0.001), irrigation volume (16 vs 24 l; p < 0.001), and improved core temperature maintenance (+0.1 °C vs -0.1 °C; p < 0.001), with higher median enucleation efficiency (1.22 vs 1.0; p = 0.003) and not statistically different operative time, complications, and functional improvement. Limitations include the inability to blind the surgeon and limited power for uncommon events. CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS: MiLEP seems to improve early continence recovery, supporting miniaturization as a strategy to enhance patient-centered outcomes after HoLEP.

global_hot_topics.abstract: Centanafadine is a multimodal norepinephrine-dopamine-serotonin reuptake inhibitor (NDSRI) that has been evaluated for the treatment of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) across pediatric, adolescent, and adult populations. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of centanafadine compared with placebo, with particular emphasis on dose-response patterns across different age groups. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) were searched from database inception to July 2026. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials evaluating centanafadine in patients with ADHD were eligible for inclusion. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool was used to assess the risk of bias. Because of differences in populations, formulations, dosing regimens, outcome measures, and reported effect estimates, findings were synthesized narratively rather than quantitatively. Four randomized trials reported in three publications, including 1845 randomized participants, were included. In children, high-dose centanafadine significantly improved attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder rating scale, version 5 (ADHD-RS-5) scores compared with placebo (-16.3 vs. -10.8; p < 0.001), whereas the low-dose group did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference (mean difference [MD] -2.7; 95% confidence interval [CI], -6.0 to 0.5; p = 0.10). In adolescents, 328.8 mg significantly improved ADHD-RS-5 scores compared with placebo (-18.5 vs. -14.2; p = 0.0006; Cohen's d = -0.40), whereas 164.4 mg did not (p = 0.3016). In adults, both 200 and 400 mg/day significantly improved Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale (AISRS) scores, with LSMDs ranging from -2.74 to -4.42 (p ≤ 0.039). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 25%-39% of children, 23.8%-50.3% of adolescents, and 17.6%-31.8% of adults, with higher rates generally observed at higher doses in some populations. Centanafadine demonstrated improvement in core ADHD symptoms across pediatric, adolescent, and adult populations, with a more apparent dose-response pattern in children and adolescents and significant efficacy across the adult doses evaluated. Higher doses were associated with increased treatment-emergent adverse events in some populations. However, the evidence base remains limited to four randomized trials from three publications, with predominantly short-term follow-up, no active-comparator trials, and limited independently sponsored evidence. Therefore, the efficacy, safety, and dose-response findings should be interpreted cautiously. Longer term, independently sponsored, and head-to-head comparative trials are needed to further establish the optimal dosing, comparative effectiveness, and long-term safety of centanafadine.

global_hot_topics.abstract: Suicidal ideation, depressive symptoms, anxiety, and sleep disturbance remain difficult to manage in psychiatric populations, and intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) has emerged as an accelerated, non-invasive neuromodulation strategy for these outcomes. This meta-analysis compares iTBS versus sham-iTBS across suicidal ideation, depression severity, anxiety severity, and sleep quality to guide clinical decision-making. We systematically searched relevant electronic databases in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Continuous outcomes were pooled as standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals using random-effects inverse-variance models in RevMan 5.4. Heterogeneity was assessed using I 2 and χ 2 statistics, and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were performed. A p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Six studies were included. iTBS significantly reduced suicidal ideation versus sham-iTBS (SMD = -0.51; 95% CI: -0.93 to -0.09; p = 0.02; I 2 = 70%; n = 181 vs. 157), and the effect remained significant with lower heterogeneity after exclusion of Qin et al. (p = 0.02; I 2 = 29%). Depression severity improved with iTBS (SMD = -1.06; 95% CI: -1.64 to -0.48; p = 0.0003; I 2 = 80%; n = 162 vs. 142), with heterogeneity decreasing to 24% after exclusion of Huang et al. Anxiety severity also improved (SMD = -0.68; 95% CI: -1.27 to -0.09; p = 0.02; I 2 = 79%; n = 139 vs. 120), and heterogeneity decreased to 38% after exclusion of Huang et al. Sleep quality did not differ significantly between groups (SMD = -0.32; 95% CI: -0.98 to 0.34; p = 0.35; I 2 = 67%; n = 75 vs. 49), based on two trials. iTBS was associated with a reduction in suicidal ideation compared with sham stimulation, but the small evidence base and between-study heterogeneity limit certainty. Secondary analyses suggested improvements in depression and anxiety severity, whereas sleep quality did not differ between groups. Larger, standardized randomized controlled trials with longer follow-up are needed to determine the magnitude and durability of any antisuicidal effect.

global_hot_topics.title: Index-window C-reactive protein and carcinoembryonic antigen and five-year all-cause mortality in Hispanic/Latino and non-Hispanic White patients with colorectal cancer: a retrospective biomarker cohort study.
global_hot_topics.abstract: AIMS: To examine index-window carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), C-reactive protein (CRP), and five-year recorded mortality by ethnicity in colorectal cancer. PATIENTS AND METHODS: This retrospective University of California Health Data Warehouse cohort included Hispanic/Latino and non-Hispanic White adults indexed during 2012-2020 with both biomarkers measured within ±30 days and complete covariates. Linear regression modeled log(CEA + 0.1); Cox regression modeled recorded all-cause mortality. RESULTS: Among 345 patients, 143 deaths were recorded. Hispanic/Latino ethnicity was associated with higher log(CEA + 0.1) (β = 0.743; robust 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.202-1.285; P = 0.007). The mortality association was nonsignificant (hazard ratio [HR], 0.723; 95% CI, 0.483-1.084; P = 0.117). Higher log(CEA + 0.1) (HR, 1.266; 95% CI, 1.174-1.366; P < 0.001) and log(CRP + 0.1) (HR, 1.134; 95% CI, 1.037-1.239; P = 0.006) were associated with mortality. CONCLUSIONS: In this biomarker-selected cohort, Hispanic/Latino patients had higher recorded CEA without a statistically significant ethnic-group mortality difference. Confirmation requires clinically characterized cohorts with stage, treatment, biomarker timing, verified assay comparability, and complete mortality ascertainment. We studied two blood tests recorded near a colorectal cancer diagnosis: carcinoembryonic antigen, which is used in cancer care, and C-reactive protein, which reflects inflammation. We examined records from 345 adults in the University of California Health system, including 95 Hispanic/Latino and 250 non-Hispanic White patients. All had both tests recorded within 30 days before or after their earliest recorded cancer diagnosis. Hispanic/Latino patients had higher recorded carcinoembryonic antigen after accounting for age, sex, and body mass index. Higher values of both tests were associated with more recorded deaths over five years. We did not detect a statistically significant difference in recorded mortality between the ethnic groups. The study included a selected group whose doctors had ordered both tests. Cancer stage, treatment, and timing of surgery were unavailable, test measurements could not be independently checked for comparability across laboratories, and deaths outside the health system may have been missed. These limitations make the clinical meaning of the group differences uncertain. Further studies need more complete clinical information and follow-up to determine whether the findings apply more broadly.

global_hot_topics.title: Single-cell imaging reveals a key role of Bck2 in yeast cell size adaptation to nutrient challenges.
global_hot_topics.authors: Yagya Chadha; Igor V Kukhtevich; Timon Stegmaier; Francesco Padovani; Robert Schneider; Kurt M Schmoller
global_hot_topics.abstract: Cell size is tightly controlled to optimize cell function. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, multiple regulators of cell size in steady-state conditions have been identified, such as the G1/S activators Cln3 and Bck2 and the inhibitor Whi5. Individual deletions of these regulators alter the mean cell volumes. However, size homeostasis remains largely intact. Here, we show that although the roles of Bck2 and Cln3 for cell size regulation appear largely redundant in steady state, a switch from fermentable to nonfermentable growth media reveals a unique role for Bck2 in cell size adaptation. We use live-cell microscopy and machine learning-assisted image analysis to track single cells and their progeny through the nutrient switch. We find that after the switch, bck2Δ cells experience longer cell cycle arrests and more arrest-associated enlargement than wild-type, whi5Δ, or cln3Δ cells, indicating that Bck2 becomes the critical G1/S activator in changing nutrients. Our work demonstrates that studying size regulation during nutrient shifts can resolve apparent redundancies observed in steady state.

global_hot_topics.title: TOMM5 is associated with oral cancer progression: a multi-omics analysis from single-cell atlas to in vitro validation.
global_hot_topics.authors: Li Gao; Jian-Di Li; Yi-Yang Chen; Ge-Li Tan; Jian-Jia Zeng; Xi Lin; Lu Liang; Shuang Xia
global_hot_topics.abstract: AIMS: Translocase of Outer Mitochondrial Membrane 5 (TOMM5), a mitochondrial outer membrane translocase subunit implicated in tumorigenesis, remains unexplored in oral cancer. Herein, we aimed to decipher the role of TOMM5 in oral cancer. METHODS: This study comprehensively explored the expression profile, clinical significance, and functional roles of TOMM5 in oral carcinogenesis with global RNA-seq and microarray datasets. In vitro experiments were performed for evaluating the impact of TOMM5 knockdown on the biological functions of oral cancer cells. Distribution heterogeneity of TOMM5 expression and related cellular trajectory was analyzed through scRNA-seq. The therapeutic implications of TOMM5 for oral cancer were analyzed through drug sensitivity prediction and tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion (TIDE) scoring. RESULTS: TOMM5 was significantly overexpressed in oral cancer tissues and demonstrated moderate diagnostic accuracy. TOMM5 knockdown significantly suppressed aggressive biological behaviors of oral cancer cells. ScRNA-seq data revealed predominant TOMM5 expression in B cells, decreasing with differentiation, and linked distinct pathway activities to specific cellular compartments. High TOMM5 expression was linked to reduced immune cell infiltration and sensitivity to Paclitaxel/Vincristine. CONCLUSIONS: Overexpressed TOMM5 shows potential as a biomarker in oral cancer, correlating with tumor progression and immune infiltration. Oral cancer remains a major health challenge with stagnant survival rates, highlighting the need for better biomarkers and therapeutic targets. We investigated TOMM5, a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, in oral cancer using transcriptomic data from over 300 tumors and normal tissues, along with functional experiments in cancer cells. Our results showed that TOMM5 is significantly overexpressed in oral cancer tissues and that high expression predicts poorer overall and disease‑free survival. Silencing TOMM5 in WSU‑HN30 oral cancer cells reduced their migratory and invasive abilities, without affecting proliferation. Single‑cell RNA sequencing revealed that TOMM5 is predominantly expressed in B cells within the tumor microenvironment and declines with cell differentiation. High TOMM5 expression correlated with reduced immune infiltration, particularly activated mast cells and neutrophils, and with increased myeloid‑derived suppressor cells, suggesting an immunosuppressive role. Furthermore, patients with elevated TOMM5 showed predicted sensitivity to paclitaxel and vincristine. In summary, TOMM5 overexpression is associated with tumor progression, immune modulation, and drug response in oral cancer, making it a promising biomarker and potential therapeutic guide. Additional experimental validation is warranted to confirm these findings.

global_hot_topics.title: Impact of healthcare setting on survival in adults with acute lymphoblastic leukemia in Latin America: insights from a large multinational cohort.
global_hot_topics.authors: Wellington F Silva; Marcela Espinoza; Luciana Ferrari; Isolda Fernández; Bruno Kosa Lino Duarte; Fabio Kerbauy; Eduardo Chapchap; André Dias Américo
global_hot_topics.abstract: BACKGROUND: Outcomes of adults with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in Latin America remain poorly characterized, particularly across public and private healthcare systems. In this study, we evaluated overall survival (OS) and relapse rates in a multinational cohort, aiming to identify key factors associated with these outcomes. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed patients aged ≥15 years with newly diagnosed ALL treated at 45 centers in Brazil, Argentina, and Chile between 2015 and 2023. Overall survival (OS) and event-free survival (EFS) were estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods. Cox models incorporating country as a shared frailty term evaluated factors associated with mortality. FINDINGS: Among 1121 patients, median age was 34 years, 56.1% were male, 81.4% had B-lineage ALL, and 24.7% had Philadelphia chromosome-positive (Ph-positive) ALL. Overall, 53% were treated in public centers. Induction mortality was higher in public than private settings (10.0% vs. 1.2%; p < 0.0001), whereas hematopoietic stem cell transplantation was less frequent (18.1% vs. 46.6%; p < 0.0001). At a median follow-up of 36.2 months, 3-year OS and EFS were 49.9% and 41.1%, respectively. Three-year OS was 42.9% in public and 57.6% in private centers (p < 0.0001). Private healthcare remained independently associated with lower mortality overall (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.42-0.68) and across major subgroups. Three-year relapse incidence was 43.9%. Among Ph-negative adolescents and young adults, male sex and leukocytosis were independently associated with increased mortality. In Ph-positive ALL, upfront dasatinib was associated with improved OS, primarily through lower non-relapse mortality rather than reduced relapse incidence. INTERPRETATION: Survival of adults with ALL in Latin America has improved compared with historical reports, but substantial disparities persist between public and private settings. Our findings support prioritizing investment in public-sector supportive care, diagnostic and treatment infrastructure, timely access to transplantation, and equitable availability of effective therapies as key strategies to improve survival across the region. medical_news.abstract: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.
